prompt.context: Our client is a for-profit, specialty college named Chic Cosmetology University (CCU). Founded in 2005, CCU is a program for high school graduates seeking their professional cosmetology license. CCU is currently the market leader for cosmetology education with campuses in ten major metropolitan areas in the US.
prompt.question: CCU has capital to invest in a new campus and is considering Chicagoland as a location — should they do it?

clarifying_info.q: How do we define a successful launch?
clarifying_info.a: The client considers a successful launch as achieving positive operating profit for the new campus two years after opening.
Enrolled students take classes at a physical campus for one school year to earn their degree. The fiscal year begins on September 1.
CCU boasts the best campuses in the industry with state-of-the-art equipment and strong job placement due to CCU's relationships with top salons in local areas.

clarifying_info.q: What is the enrollment growth trend?
clarifying_info.a: CCU and industry enrollments are growing at 5% per year.
There are 2-3 other large specialty colleges, some of which are in the same geographies as CCU. Community colleges are also beginning to offer cosmetology degrees at lower prices.

clarifying_info.q: How long have existing CCU campuses been operating?
clarifying_info.a: All ten CCU campuses have been present for at least three full school years. All competitor campuses have also been present for similar lengths of time.

clarifying_info.q: What are the industry entry requirements?
clarifying_info.a: A high school diploma and cosmetology degree are required to enter the field. 98% of cosmetologists are women.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost to build the new Chicago campus?
clarifying_info.a: The total cost is $4.5M in initial building costs to renovate its chosen site. These costs can be amortized evenly over a three-year period. Assume fixed costs remain flat per year.

exhibits.title: 2010 CCU Financials
exhibits.shows: A financial summary table for CCU as of 8/31/2010, reported in thousands of dollars, covering all ten campuses.

exhibits.title: CCU and Major Competitor Campus Locations
exhibits.shows: A table listing ten CCU campus cities with their 2010 market share (measured as share of total potential students as defined by CCU), alongside a map legend showing CCU campus markers and major competitor campus markers.

data.Note: Share measured as share of total potential students as defined by CCU; data as of 8/31/2010

framework: 1. Evaluate CCU revenue and cost structures (revenue per student, fixed cost per campus, variable cost per student, gross profit per student)
2. Determine break-even enrollment for the Chicago campus, incorporating initial investment amortization
3. Estimate the total addressable market in Chicagoland (HS segment + adult segment)
4. Project CCU Chicago's realistic market share based on competitive dynamics from existing campuses
5. Compare projected Year 1 enrollments to break-even enrollment and assess feasibility
6. Identify qualitative issues and alternatives if the numbers do not support entry

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 1, what are the key unit economics for a CCU campus?
questions.guidance: Candidate should divide aggregate figures by number of campuses/students: average revenue per enrollment = $15K ($150M / 10,000); total annual fixed cost per campus = $4.8M ($48M / 10); total variable cost per student = $8K ($80M / 10,000); gross profit per student = $7K ($15K - $8K).

math.setup: All figures from Exhibit 1 divided by 10 campuses or 10,000 students as appropriate.
math.answer: Revenue per student: $15K; Fixed cost per campus: $4.8M; Variable cost per student: $8K; Gross profit per student: $7K

questions.prompt: What is the break-even number of students required for the Chicago campus in Year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate must add the annual amortization of the $4.5M build cost (over 3 years = $1.5M/year) to the $4.8M campus fixed cost to get total annual fixed cost of $6.3M, then divide by $7K gross profit per student.

math.setup: Total annual fixed cost = campus fixed cost + amortization. Break-even = total annual fixed cost / gross profit per student.

questions.prompt: What types of schools and students does CCU target? How many potential students are in the Chicagoland market?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify: public/middle-class high schools (geography, affordability), female HS graduates not attending 4-year college, interested in cosmetology. Interviewer reveals: 1,000 targeted HS in Chicagoland, ~6 potential students per HS. Candidate should also derive the adult market (20% of enrolled students are from adult market, so adult potential = HS potential x 25%). Total potential = 6,000 (HS) + 1,500 (adult) = 7,500.

math.setup: HS potential = 6 students/HS x 1,000 HS. Adult potential derived from fact that 80% of students come from HS and 20% from adult market, implying adult pool = HS pool x (20/80) = HS pool x 25%.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what market share should CCU Chicago expect to capture in Year 1, and what does that mean for projected enrollments?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: campuses without competitors average ~15% share (Minneapolis 15%, Dallas 14%, Atlanta 16%, NYC 16%); campuses with one competitor tend to average ~10-12% (Houston 10%, Philly 12%, Miami 12%); Boston has 8% share with only one competitor — but candidate should note these campuses have all operated 3+ years, so Chicago (new) is unlikely to hit mature-market share in Year 1. The reasonable assumption is 10% for a city with one competitor. Year 1 enrollment = 7,500 x 10% = 750. Year 2 enrollment = 750 x 1.05 = ~788.

math.setup: Projected enrollment = total potential students x projected market share.
steps: Projected market share = 10% (one competitor present; mature campuses show 10%)

questions.prompt: (Bonus, if time permits) Suppose CCU finds an alternative lot with a one-time construction cost of $300K (same amortization schedule). Does this change the recommendation?
questions.guidance: New amortization = $300K / 3 = $100K/year. New total fixed cost = $4.8M + $0.1M = $4.9M. New break-even = $4.9M / $7K = 700 students. Year 1 projection is still 750, which exceeds 700 — so the numbers suggest entry is feasible. However, an excellent candidate will note that the 10% market share benchmark is from campuses operating 3+ years; a new Chicago campus is unlikely to achieve 10% in Year 1 or 2, making even 700 difficult to reach reliably.

math.setup: New break-even = (fixed cost + new amortization) / gross profit per student.
math.answer: New break-even: 700 students. Year 1 projection of 750 technically exceeds this, but market share ramp-up risk makes it borderline.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative factors should CCU consider as it evaluates the Chicago opportunity and alternative paths forward?

categories.name: Target schools and students
ideas: Public high schools in middle-class Chicagoland suburbs (private HS grads more likely to pursue 4-year universities)
Schools geographically close to the proposed campus
Female graduates who are not planning to attend a 4-year college
Students with demonstrated interest in beauty/cosmetology

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: One established competitor already in Chicago — mature share may be suppressed to ~10% or lower for new entrant
Community colleges offering cosmetology at lower price points could erode price-sensitive segment
New campus will take time to build brand and salon relationships in local market

categories.name: Ways to increase enrollments or reduce break-even
ideas: Offer scholarships to increase conversion rate of potential students
Reduce fixed costs by transporting equipment/materials from under-capacity existing campuses
Negotiate lower facility lease or renovation costs

categories.name: Alternative market expansion strategies
ideas: Consider other US cities without a CCU presence where potential-per-HS may be higher
Add a second campus in a high-share city such as NYC to expand capacity where brand is proven
Conduct deeper market research across cities to compare ROI before committing to Chicago

recommendation: CCU should NOT enter the Chicago market under the current $4.5M cost structure. Even under optimistic assumptions (10% market share), Year 1 enrollment is projected at 750 students — 150 short of the 900 break-even. Year 2 enrollment of ~788 also falls short. The campus would not achieve positive operating profit within two years, failing the client's own success criterion.

If CCU can secure the alternative $300K construction site, the break-even drops to 700 students, which is technically within reach of the 750 projection. However, this marginal case relies on achieving mature-market share levels (10%) in Year 1, which is unrealistic given that all benchmarked campuses took at least three years to reach their current share. The recommendation remains to not proceed without a more favorable demand or cost scenario.
risks: Market share ramp-up is slower than mature-campus benchmarks imply — Year 1 share is likely below 10%
Community college competition may further compress addressable market and pricing power
A single competitor in Chicago could respond aggressively to protect share, suppressing CCU's ramp even further
next_steps: Conduct market research in other Chicagoland or alternative-city markets to identify locations with higher potential-per-HS
Evaluate scholarship programs or alternative pricing to increase the pool of likely enrollees
Assess whether equipment can be shared from under-capacity campuses to lower the fixed cost base
Revisit in 1-2 years if brand awareness in Chicagoland grows organically or competitor dynamics shift
